name: Ahinoam of Jezreel
title: David's wife from Jezreel
summary: Ahinoam from Jezreel was one of King David's earliest wives, whom he took as his wife during the period when he lived as an outlaw and was pursued by King Saul. She is consistently mentioned together with Abigail from Carmel, and the two women shared a fate throughout David's wandering life. Ahinoam was captured by Amalekites during the raid on Ziklag, but she was rescued when David pursued the enemy and freed the captives. After Saul's death, she followed David to Hebron, where he was anointed king over Judah. In Hebron she gave birth to Amnon, David's firstborn son – a son whose tragic life would later cast dark shadows over the royal house.

keyEvents.title: Marriage to David
keyEvents.description: David married Ahinoam of Jezreel during the time he was fleeing from Saul. She became his wife along with Abigail from Carmel.

keyEvents.title: Captured by the Amalekites
keyEvents.description: Ahinoam was taken captive together with Abigail when the Amalekites attacked and plundered Ziklag. David pursued the attackers and rescued both wives as well as all other captives.

keyEvents.title: Follows David to Hebron
keyEvents.description: After Saul's death, Ahinoam went with David to Hebron, where he was anointed king over Judah.

keyEvents.title: Bears Amnon
keyEvents.description: In Hebron, Ahinoam bore Amnon, who became David's firstborn son.

versions.summary: Ahinoam of Jezreel was one of King David's first wives, whom he married while fleeing from King Saul. She was the mother of Amnon, David's firstborn son. She faithfully followed David through his years as a fugitive and into the kingdom.
versions.title: David's First Wife
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'David's first wife' is somewhat imprecise. The Bible states that Saul gave his daughter Michal to David as a wife before Ahinoam. Thus, Ahinoam was not David's first wife, but one of his early wives. The title should be adjusted.; [major] The role 'queen' is imprecise. Ahinoam is never explicitly called queen in the Bible. She was David's wife/spouse. More appropriate roles would be 'wife' and 'mother'.; [major] The summary describes Ahinoam as 'one of King David's first wives', but the phrasing could give the impression that she was the very first. Michal was David's first wife (1 Sam 18:27). Furthermore, Amnon is called 'David's firstborn son', which is correct, but it should be clarified that this refers to his firstborn in Hebron/by Ahinoam.; [minor] The description states that Amnon was 'heir to the throne', but this is an interpretation not directly supported by the text. Amnon never became heir in a practical sense, and he was killed by Absalom (2 Sam 13). The phrasing should be adjusted.; [major] Footnotes are missing. Notes should be added regarding the linguistic aspect of the name Ahinoam, the geographical significance of Jezreel, and the possible connection to Saul's wife with the same name.

versions.summary: Ahinoam of Jezreel was one of King David's early wives, whom he married while fleeing from King Saul. She is often mentioned together with Abigail of Carmel. Ahinoam was the mother of Amnon, David's firstborn son, who was born in Hebron. She faithfully followed David through his years as a fugitive, was captured by the Amalekites from Ziklag and then rescued, and continued to follow him into his kingship in Hebron.
versions.title: David's wife from Jezreel
versions.reason: [minor] The summary is good but could be improved with a bit more theological depth and variety from the previous version. The phrasing about "faithful" is an interpretation not directly supported by the text – the Bible says nothing about her attitude, only that she went along.; [minor] The third footnote stating that Saul's wife was named Ahinoam is interesting, but categorizing it as "theological" is somewhat misleading. Speculation about identity is primarily a historical/academic hypothesis, not theological. Change to "historical".; [minor] The role of "refugee" or "prisoner of war" could have been relevant given that she was taken captive by the Amalekites and lived as a refugee with David, but this is not necessarily a fixed "role." The current roles are sufficient.

footnotes.text: The name Ahinoam (אֲחִינֹעַם) means 'my brother is pleasant' or 'my brother is gracious' in Hebrew, composed of 'ach' (brother) and 'noam' (pleasantness/grace).

Jezreel was a city in the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:56), not to be confused with the more well-known Jezreel Valley in the north. Ahinoam thus came from a small town in the hill country of Judah, near David's home region.

Saul's wife was also named Ahinoam (1 Sam 14:50). Some scholars have speculated whether this could have been the same person, which would have had significant political and symbolic implications for David's claim to legitimacy, but this remains an unconfirmed hypothesis.

David's marriage to Ahinoam during his time as a fugitive may have carried political overtones. Marrying women from different clans in Judah strengthened his alliances and position ahead of his reign as king in Hebron.

Amnon, Ahinoam's son and David's firstborn, was later killed by his half-brother Absalom after he raped his half-sister Tamar (2 Sam 13). The tragic fate of the firstborn has been a subject of theological reflection on the consequences of sin in David's house.
